content: Pelvic Organ Prolapse (POP) is a condition where one or more of the pelvic organs—including the bladder, uterus, vagina, small bowel, or rectum—descend from their normal anatomical position into or outside the vaginal canal. This occurs due to weakening or injury of the pelvic floor muscles and connective tissues that normally provide support. Mechanisms include childbirth trauma, aging, hormonal changes, chronic increased intra-abdominal pressure, and genetic predisposition. POP can severely impact quality of life, causing symptoms such as a vaginal bulge sensation, pelvic pressure, urinary and bowel dysfunction, and sexual discomfort. Major synonyms include pelvic floor prolapse and genital prolapse. Diagnosis is generally clinical but may utilize imaging such as ultrasound or MRI for complex cases. Management ranges from conservative approaches—such as pelvic floor muscle training and pessary use—to surgical repair. Limitations of current treatments include variable long-term efficacy and recurrence risk. Safety considerations involve risks of surgery, pessary complications, and the need for individualized treatment plans. Understanding POP is crucial for early recognition, appropriate referral, and patient-centered management. This module provides comprehensive, evidence-calibrated insights to assist patients and healthcare workers in understanding, preventing, diagnosing, and managing pelvic organ prolapse.

content: Pelvic organ prolapse (POP) occurs when the structures that support pelvic organs like the bladder, uterus, vagina, rectum, and small bowel weaken or become damaged. This causes one or more organs to drop, bulging into the vaginal area. The severity can range from mild discomfort to a visible bulge outside the vagina. POP is sometimes also called pelvic floor prolapse or genital prolapse. It is a common condition that affects women, especially with increasing age and following childbirth.

chunk_title: Anatomy and Physiology of the Pelvic Floor
content: The pelvic floor is composed of muscles, ligaments, and connective tissue that support pelvic organs in their normal positions inside the pelvis. Key muscles include the levator ani group, which acts like a hammock. Connective tissue such as endopelvic fascia stabilizes the organs. Proper muscle tone and ligament strength are crucial for maintaining continence and pelvic organ position. Injury or weakness reduces support, predisposing to prolapse.

content: Main risk factors for POP include vaginal childbirth, aging, menopause with declining estrogen, obesity, chronic coughing or constipation causing pressure, heavy lifting, hysterectomy, and genetics. Childbirth-related trauma is a significant contributor, especially multiple vaginal births or traumatic deliveries. Menopause triggers tissue atrophy and loss of collagen. High intra-abdominal pressure from chronic strain also stresses pelvic supports.

content: Many women with POP experience symptoms such as a sensation of pelvic pressure or heaviness, visible or palpable bulge at or beyond the vaginal opening, urinary symptoms including urgency, frequency, incontinence, difficulty emptying the bladder, bowel symptoms such as constipation or incomplete evacuation, and sexual dysfunction like discomfort or reduced sensation. Some women remain asymptomatic and discover the prolapse on routine exam.

content: Diagnosis of POP is primarily clinical, involving pelvic examination where the degree and compartments of prolapse (anterior, apical, posterior) are assessed using standardized systems like the Pelvic Organ Prolapse Quantification (POP-Q) system. Urinary and bowel function should be evaluated through history and potentially urodynamic studies. Imaging such as ultrasound or MRI can aid in complex cases or surgical planning but is not routinely required.

content: Conservative treatment includes pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT), which strengthens the supportive muscles, and pelvic floor physical therapy techniques. The use of vaginal pessaries—devices inserted to mechanically support organs—is common for symptom relief, especially in women wishing to avoid surgery or with contraindications. Lifestyle measures such as weight loss, constipation management, and avoiding heavy lifting are important adjuncts.

review_status: AI draft - scientific, clinical, and editorial review required
content: Surgery is considered for women with symptomatic POP who do not improve with conservative management or have significant prolapse impacting quality of life. Techniques vary based on the prolapsed compartment and patient preference, including native tissue repairs and use of synthetic or biologic grafts. Approaches include vaginal, abdominal (open or laparoscopic), or robotic-assisted procedures. Each has benefits and risks, including recurrence and possible complications.

content: Safety considerations include surgical risks such as bleeding, infection, mesh complications (if synthetic material is used), nerve damage, and recurrence of prolapse. Pessary use may cause vaginal irritation or discharge; regular follow-up for cleaning and assessment is essential. Pelvic floor exercises are generally safe but should be performed correctly to avoid worsening symptoms. Decisions should be individualized based on patient factors and preferences.

content: Prevention focuses on modifiable factors such as maintaining healthy weight, avoiding excessive heavy lifting, treating chronic cough or constipation, and performing pelvic floor exercises regularly especially postpartum. Early pelvic floor rehabilitation after childbirth can reduce risk. Education on proper body mechanics during daily activities also helps reduce strain on the pelvic floor.

chunk_title: Common Misconceptions about Pelvic Organ Prolapse
content: A frequent misconception is that pelvic organ prolapse always requires surgery; many cases can be managed conservatively. Some believe it invariably causes severe symptoms, but mild prolapse can be asymptomatic. Another incorrect belief is that only older women develop prolapse; younger women, especially after childbirth, can be affected. Understanding these misconceptions aids in patient education and adherence to management plans.

chunk_title: Impact on Quality of Life and Sexual Function
content: POP can adversely affect quality of life by causing discomfort, urinary or bowel dysfunction, and emotional distress. Sexual function may be impaired by prolapse-related pain, fear of discomfort, or altered anatomy, resulting in reduced intimacy and self-esteem. Addressing these aspects through counseling and tailored treatment improves overall wellbeing.
